His career nearly ended before it had properly begun. At 18, Kaká suffered a spinal fracture in an accident at a swimming pool. - **2007 Ballon d’Or** and **FIFA World Player of the Year**

### Why the Manchester City transfer mattered
In January 2009, shortly after Manchester City had been bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group, City pursued Kaká with a reported offer of roughly **£100 million**—figures varied by report—which would have shattered the world transfer record at the time. The proposed salary was also extraordinary.

- Signaled City’s ambition to move rapidly from a mid-table club to a global superpower

- Provoked strong opposition from Milan supporters, who gathered to urge Kaká to stay

# Who really is Kaka?

In January 2009, Manchester City tried to turn football’s new financial order into a single, spectacular transaction. The club’s Abu Dhabi owners authorized an extraordinary attempt to sign AC Milan’s Brazilian playmaker Kaka, with reports valuing the proposed transfer at roughly **$150 million**—around £100 million at the time—and the player’s prospective wages at an equally astonishing level.

The figures varied depending on the source, but the message was unmistakable. City, recently purchased by Sheikh Mansour and already responsible for the dramatic signing of Robinho, wanted to prove that no footballer—and perhaps no club—was beyond its reach.

Yet Kaka was not just another superstar. To understand why the proposed move caused such fascination, it is necessary to ask a more basic question: Who really is Kaka?

## From Brasília to the world stage

Kaka was born Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite in Brasília on April 22, 1982. His famous nickname came from his younger brother’s childhood difficulty pronouncing “Ricardo.” Unlike many Brazilian footballers whose biographies begin in extreme poverty, Kaka grew up in a financially comfortable, stable family. His father was an engineer, and his mother worked as a teacher.

That background sometimes made him appear unusual within football’s familiar rags-to-riches narratives. So did his personality. Kaka was polished, reserved and openly religious, often celebrating victories by pointing toward the sky. His shirts carrying the phrase “I Belong to Jesus” became nearly as recognizable as his long strides through midfield.

His path to the top, however, was not without danger. As a teenager, Kaka suffered a spinal injury in a swimming-pool accident. He recovered fully, something he later described through the lens of his Christian faith, but the episode gave his career a sense of fragility and purpose.

Kaka joined São Paulo’s youth system and made his senior breakthrough in 2001. He was soon regarded as one of Brazil’s brightest talents: not quite a traditional number 10 and not simply a midfielder, but a player who could receive the ball deep, accelerate past opponents and finish like a forward.

He was part of Brazil’s World Cup-winning squad in 2002, although he played only a small role in the tournament. The experience nevertheless placed him alongside Ronaldo, Rivaldo, Ronaldinho, Roberto Carlos and Cafu—and confirmed that his future belonged on football’s largest stages.

## Becoming Milan’s golden boy

AC Milan signed Kaka in 2003 for a fee that soon looked like one of the bargains of the decade. He adapted to Italian football with remarkable speed, displacing Rui Costa and becoming central to Carlo Ancelotti’s sophisticated side.

At his best, Kaka made elite football look unusually simple. He did not depend on elaborate tricks. His great weapon was movement: a sudden change of pace, a direct run through the center of the pitch, a perfectly weighted pass or a composed finish after carrying the ball 40 yards.

With Milan, he won Serie A in his first season. He helped the club reach the 2005 Champions League final, where Milan surrendered a three-goal lead and lost to Liverpool on penalties in Istanbul. Two years later, Milan gained revenge by beating Liverpool in Athens.

The 2006–07 Champions League campaign was Kaka’s masterpiece. He finished as the competition’s leading scorer and produced defining performances during Milan’s run to the trophy, including a memorable goal against Manchester United at Old Trafford. In 2007, he won both the FIFA World Player of the Year award and the Ballon d’Or.

For a brief period, before Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo established their long duopoly, Kaka was widely considered the best footballer in the world.

## Why Manchester City wanted him

By January 2009, City’s pursuit was about much more than solving a tactical problem.

The club had been transformed by its takeover in September 2008. Robinho’s arrival from Real Madrid on the final day of the summer transfer window announced City’s ambition, but Kaka would have represented something larger: instant entry into football’s aristocracy.

At that point, City were not yet a Champions League club or even a consistent domestic contender. They were attempting to persuade the reigning Ballon d’Or holder to leave one of Europe’s grandest institutions for a project based largely on future promises.

For Milan, the reported fee was difficult to ignore. It could have reshaped the squad and eased financial pressures. Club executives appeared willing to discuss a sale, even as supporters gathered near Kaka’s home and demanded that their idol remain.

Kaka eventually stayed. He appeared at a window holding a Milan shirt, a gesture interpreted as a declaration of loyalty. The proposed transfer collapsed amid questions about negotiations, contracts, sporting ambition and whether the player genuinely wanted the move.

For many supporters, his refusal offered a rare romantic victory over money. Here was a footballer who seemingly chose history, affection and competitive credibility over an unprecedented salary.

## Loyalty, ambition—or timing?

The story became more complicated only a few months later.

In June 2009, Kaka left Milan for Real Madrid in a transfer worth approximately €67 million. The move did not make his rejection of City meaningless: Real were already among football’s established powers, and joining them offered immediate prestige and Champions League competition. Milan also needed the money, while Kaka’s physical condition had begun to attract concern.

Still, the Madrid transfer changed the interpretation. Kaka had not decided to remain at Milan forever. He had decided not to join Manchester City at that moment.

His years in Spain were disrupted by injuries, including persistent knee problems. He contributed to a league title and other successes, but he never consistently reproduced his 2007 form. In a team increasingly defined by Ronaldo, Kaka became a supporting figure rather than its central star.

He returned to Milan in 2013, later played for São Paulo on loan and finished his career with Orlando City in Major League Soccer. He retired in 2017 as a World Cup winner, Champions League winner and Ballon d’Or recipient—one of the most accomplished players of his generation.

## The man behind the price

The $150 million pursuit helped make Kaka a symbol in an argument that was never solely about him. It was about whether new wealth could purchase status, whether loyalty still mattered and whether a footballer should be judged for accepting an offer almost no ordinary person could imagine refusing.

Kaka’s image encouraged people to cast him as the virtuous alternative to football’s excesses: religious, devoted to his family and seemingly uninterested in becoming the highest-paid player alive. But he was also an ambitious professional whose career choices involved agents, clubs, injuries, sporting goals and financial realities.

Perhaps that is who Kaka really was—not a saint rejecting money, nor a mercenary waiting for a more prestigious offer, but a great player trying to balance affection for Milan with the limited span of an elite career.

With hindsight, City soon became one of the dominant forces in English football, while Kaka’s move to Madrid never reached the heights expected of it. Had he joined City, he might have become the face of their revolution. He might also have spent his prime years carrying an unfinished team outside the Champions League.

So the question remains: **Should Kaka have stayed with Milan and protected the bond he had built there—or should he have taken Manchester City’s money and become the first true icon of a new football empire?**
